claims.text: Element identity in CrFeCoNiX alloys governs oxidation-induced surface and oxide-film evolution through element-specific environmental interactions and thermodynamic tendencies.
Al is a highly stable, slow-growing oxide former in CrFeCoNiAl.
An alumina scale formed on CrFeCoNiAl above 900 °C remains coherent and self-healing.
Low Al diffusivity and slow Al oxidation kinetics limit oxide growth and the mechanical mismatch responsible for cracking.
Mn and Si are less effective protective-oxide formers than Al in the CrFeCoNiX system.
Mn- or Si-containing oxides grow more rapidly than the proposed alumina scale.
Higher oxygen or cation diffusion rates and larger volumetric mismatches make Mn- or Si-rich scales prone to spallation.
Oxidation of a CoCrFeNiMn alloy in controlled oxygen produces time-dependent compositional and structural evolution of its surface oxide.
The oxide scale acts as a barrier against further oxidation.
CrFeCoNiAl forms a submicron, coherent Al2O3 layer, whereas CrFeCoNiMn and CrFeCoNiSi form thicker and less adherent oxides.
Selective oxidation and thermodynamic preferences determine which elements enrich the oxide film over time.
Limited outward Al diffusion causes slow, controlled nucleation and growth of Al2O3 on CrFeCoNiAl.
Slow alumina growth minimizes volumetric mismatch and internal stress, thereby preventing cracking and spallation.
Mn- or Si-bearing variants form less thermodynamically stable oxides or volatile species.
Under identical exposure conditions above 900 °C, CrFeCoNiAl will form a thinner, more stable, and more coherent scale than CrFeCoNiMn or CrFeCoNiSi.
The scale on CrFeCoNiAl will persist without spallation, while the Mn- and Si-containing variants will develop heterogeneous scales with cracks or spallation during prolonged exposure.
Previous work has shown less stable oxidation behavior for CrFeCoNiMn or CrFeCoNiSi than for CrFeCoNiAl.
The proposed behavior applies to equiatomic or near-equiatomic CrFeCoNiX alloys in single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution states during prolonged oxidative or corrosive exposure above 900 °C.
Transient thermal cycling or significant secondary-phase formation may change the predicted oxide behavior.
